title: Index Selectivity
description: Measure and use column selectivity to choose the best indexes

data.text: Selectivity measures how unique values are in a column. High-selectivity indexes filter many rows per seek. Low-selectivity indexes like gender or boolean flags often do not help the optimizer.

data.title: Formula
items: Close to 1: high selectivity, good for indexing
Close to 0: low selectivity, poor for indexing
Combine low-selectivity columns in composite indexes

data.title: Selectivity check
data.code:
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT email) / COUNT(*) AS email_selectivity,
  COUNT(DISTINCT status) / COUNT(*) AS status_selectivity,
  COUNT(DISTINCT country) / COUNT(*) AS country_selectivity
FROM users;

data.title: Warning
data.text: Low-selectivity indexes can still help if the query filters on a small percentage of rows. Always check the actual execution plan.

items.question: What is the selectivity threshold for indexing?
items.answer: There is no fixed threshold. Test with EXPLAIN. Values above 0.1 are usually worth indexing alone.

items.question: Can low-selectivity columns be useful in composites?
items.answer: Yes. A composite on (status, created_at) can help if status is filtered and created_at is sorted.

items.question: Does the optimizer consider selectivity?
items.answer: Yes. Most optimizers use column statistics to choose between index scans and sequential scans.

data.title: Summary
points: High-selectivity columns make good standalone indexes
data.takeaway: Selectivity guides index selection but does not replace execution plan verification.
